name: Elicit Values First
description: Begin by asking about the person’s goals, concerns, and moral priorities, then frame evidence in terms that align with those values to boost relevance and receptivity.

name: Prebunk and Inoculate

name: Ask-Tell-Ask Loop

name: Source Transparency

name: Use Concrete Narratives

name: Localize and Personalize

name: Elicit Beliefs First
description: Begin by asking the person’s current views, goals, and concerns to tailor arguments to their values and knowledge gaps.

name: Shared Goals Framing
description: Frame evidence and policies in terms of outcomes they already care about (health, prosperity, security, fairness) to reduce identity threat.

name: Credible Evidence Layering

name: Transparent Uncertainty

name: Prebunking & Inoculation
description: Proactively explain common misconceptions and why they’re misleading, then provide correct interpretations to reduce later susceptibility.

name: Local and Personal Relevance
description: Connect evidence to their local context or lived experience (e.g., regional data, personal risk/benefit) to make abstract facts salient.

name: Interactive Socratic Probing
description: Use questions to surface assumptions, test counterfactuals, and guide them to derive implications themselves, fostering internal buy-in.

name: Counter-Argument Steelmanning
description: Accurately summarize the strongest opposing views, then address them with evidence and fair comparisons of trade-offs.

name: Incremental Commitments
description: Seek small points of agreement and build upward (facts → mechanisms → implications → policy), reducing psychological reactance.

name: Choice Architecture & Defaults
description: When proposing actions, present low-friction options, defaults, or checklists that align with their preferences, converting agreement into behavior.

name: Clarify Goals Early
description: Ask the person’s aims, values, and decision context up front to tailor evidence and examples to what they care about most.

name: Elicit Prior Beliefs
description: Invite them to share their current views and reasons, so you can map areas of agreement, avoid strawmanning, and focus on true points of contention.

name: Calibrate With Shared Facts
description: Start from uncontroversial, jointly verifiable facts and definitions to establish common ground and reduce misunderstanding.

name: Layered Evidence Build
description: Present evidence in tiers—high-level consensus, key mechanisms, representative studies, and quantitative estimates—so they can dive as deep as they prefer.

name: Counter-Argument Steelman
description: Articulate the strongest version of opposing views fairly, then address them with evidence and transparent reasoning.

name: Use Causal Mechanisms
description: Explain the underlying mechanisms (how X leads to Y) to make claims intuitive and resilient to isolated counterexamples.

name: Decision-Relevant Framing
description: Translate evidence into concrete trade-offs, expected impacts, and timelines that relate directly to personal or policy choices.

name: Uncertainty With Ranges
description: Quantify uncertainty and provide credible intervals or scenario ranges to build trust and prevent overclaiming.

name: Interactive Misconception Check
description: Periodically ask brief diagnostic questions to detect misconceptions or confusion, then adapt explanations to correct them.

name: Local and Lived Examples
description: Connect abstract evidence to local data, case studies, or relatable analogies that match the person’s context and experiences.

name: Values Framing
description: Connect evidence to the person’s core values (e.g., health, fairness, freedom, stewardship) to make the conclusion feel personally relevant and morally resonant.

name: Credible Evidence Ladder
description: Start with broad scientific/economic consensus, then move to meta-analyses and landmark studies, and finally local or personalized data, escalating rigor while staying accessible.

name: Precision Empathy
description: Elicit the person’s concerns, uncertainties, and constraints, then tailor explanations and examples to those specific motivations rather than offering generic rebuttals.

name: Trade-off Transparency
description: Acknowledge costs, uncertainties, and limits openly, then compare expected benefits versus risks to build trust and demonstrate reasoned judgment.

name: Counterfactual Scenarios
description: Contrast what likely happens with and without the policy or belief (best-, base-, and worst-case), making consequences vivid and choice-sensitive.

name: Analogies and Mechanisms
description: Use simple, accurate analogies to explain causal mechanisms, then link back to the formal evidence so intuition and data reinforce each other.

name: Interactive Calibration
description: Ask for the person’s probability estimates or thresholds for changing their mind, then provide targeted evidence to meet or update those thresholds.

name: Local and Identity Messengers
description: Cite endorsements or outcomes from in-group experts, local communities, or trusted institutions to reduce perceived social and identity costs of agreement.

name: Commitment and Plan
description: After agreement on principles, invite a small, specific next step (e.g., support a policy, share a resource) to convert attitude change into durable action.

name: Calibrate to Prior Knowledge
description: Assess what they already understand or misunderstand, then tailor explanations to fill gaps without redundancy or condescension.

name: Use Layered Evidence
description: Present a clear headline claim, then offer progressively deeper evidence (summaries, key studies, meta-analyses, data visualizations) based on how much detail they request.

name: Concrete Analogies
description: Translate abstract concepts into everyday analogies or relatable examples to make mechanisms and trade-offs intuitive.

name: Local and Personal Impact
description: Connect the issue to near-term, local, or personal consequences and benefits, clarifying what changes mean for their community or household.

name: Interactive Scenario Testing
description: Invite them to propose hypotheticals or policy tweaks, then reason through expected outcomes together using models and historical benchmarks.

name: Affirm Autonomy
description: Emphasize that the decision is theirs, ask permission to share information, and offer choices in how to proceed to reduce reactance.

name: Iterative Summaries
description: Periodically recap points of agreement, open questions, and next steps, adjusting the approach based on their feedback and clarifications.

name: Confidence Calibration
description: Invite both sides to state confidence levels and what evidence could change them, then supply high-quality sources addressing those pivotal uncertainties.

name: Principle-to-Policy Bridge
description: Start from shared, uncontroversial principles (e.g., fairness, risk reduction), then show stepwise how the proposed belief or policy logically follows.

name: Steelman and Acknowledge Costs
description: Accurately restate the strongest counterarguments and acknowledge real trade-offs, then explain why the net benefits still favor the position.

name: Visual Evidence Scaffolding
description: Use simple, cumulative visuals (trends, causal diagrams, benchmarks) introduced stepwise to build from core facts to conclusions without overloading.

name: Commitment to Follow-Up
description: Offer summaries, sources, and a plan to revisit questions after they've reviewed materials, sustaining engagement and trust over multiple exchanges.

name: Calibrate Common Ground
description: Identify points of agreement and shared facts early, then build incrementally from those to reduce perceived distance and facilitate acceptance of new evidence.

name: Use Transparent Sourcing
description: Cite high-quality consensus sources (e.g., meta-analyses, systematic reviews, major academies) and explain why they’re credible, while acknowledging uncertainties and ranges.

name: Narratives with Numbers
description: Combine brief, concrete stories or case examples with key statistics to make evidence memorable without sacrificing accuracy.

name: Quantify Trade-offs
description: Frame policies in terms of explicit costs, benefits, and timelines, using comparisons and counterfactuals to clarify what happens if no action is taken.

name: Offer Testable Predictions
description: Propose near-term, observable indicators and agree to revisit them, building accountability and trust through falsifiable claims.

name: Decision-Focused Reframing
description: Translate abstract beliefs into concrete choices (e.g., what policy or behavior to support), clarifying criteria and thresholds for action.

name: Acknowledge Identity Concerns
description: Respectfully recognize group identities and moral intuitions, avoid contempt, and use identity-consistent messengers or analogies to reduce reactance.

name: Elicit Goals First
description: Begin by asking about the person’s values, priorities, and constraints to tailor evidence and framing to what they care about most.

name: Build Shared Ground
description: Identify and affirm points of agreement early to create a cooperative tone and reduce defensiveness before addressing disagreements.

name: Evidence Layering
description: Present core findings first, then progressively add details (methods, uncertainty ranges, replications) as the person asks for depth, ensuring clarity without overload.

name: Counter-Argument Prebunking
description: Anticipate common misconceptions and briefly explain why they’re misleading before they arise, inoculating against later exposure.

name: Personal Relevance Framing
description: Translate abstract evidence into concrete local or personal impacts (health, costs, risks) that map onto the person’s daily life.

name: Interactive Fact-Checking
description: Invite the person to examine sources with you in real time, summarizing key figures and methods and offering to compare alternative sources transparently.

name: Uncertainty With Boundaries
description: Acknowledge uncertainties and specify what is well-established versus still-debated, clarifying how decisions can still be made under bounded uncertainty.

name: Choice Architecture
description: Offer a small set of clear policy or belief options with trade-offs, helping the person actively choose rather than passively receive a conclusion.

name: Narratives Plus Numbers
description: Combine rigorous statistics with brief, representative case stories to make evidence memorable without overgeneralizing from anecdotes.

name: Summarize and Commit
description: Periodically recap agreed points and next questions, and ask for a small commitment (e.g., ‘Does this address your concern?’) to reinforce progress and surface remaining gaps.

name: Calibrate Baseline Knowledge
description: Assess their current understanding and misconceptions with gentle questions, then tailor explanations to fill gaps without overwhelming or talking down.

name: Present Consensus Clearly
description: Summarize the scientific or economic consensus and why experts agree, distinguishing settled points from genuine uncertainties to build trust.

name: Concrete, Localized Examples
description: Link abstract evidence to tangible, relatable cases (local impacts, everyday benefits, historical parallels) to make the stakes and mechanisms vivid.

name: Transparent Trade-offs
description: Acknowledge costs, limits, and uncertainties explicitly, then weigh them against benefits and alternatives to demonstrate fairness and rigor.

name: Prebunking and Debunking
description: Proactively explain common misconceptions and rhetorical fallacies, and when they arise, correct them with concise, evidence-backed refutations.

name: Testable Predictions
description: Offer near-term, observable predictions or decision-relevant indicators and invite follow-up, turning claims into accountable expectations.

name: Interactive Choice Architecture
description: Present multiple policy or belief framings (e.g., market-based vs. regulatory) and let the person choose a path, fostering autonomy and buy-in.

name: Narratives with Mechanisms
description: Use brief stories of people or communities affected, paired with clear causal mechanisms and data, to engage emotion without sacrificing rigor.

name: Commitment and Recap
description: Periodically summarize shared ground and ask for small, specific next steps (e.g., reading an article, revisiting a claim later) to consolidate movement.

name: Define Terms Clearly
description: Establish shared definitions (e.g., ‘risk,’ ‘effectiveness,’ ‘externality’) to prevent talking past each other and to ground later evidence.

name: Present Layered Evidence
description: Offer a concise core case first, then optional deeper layers (data, methods, caveats) so the person can engage at their preferred depth.

name: Use Trusted Messengers
description: Cite consensus statements and meta-analyses from institutions or experts the person finds credible, not just authorities you prefer.

name: Quantify Uncertainty
description: Acknowledge limitations and ranges of estimates to build trust, explaining what’s known, what’s uncertain, and why the balance of evidence favors the claim.

name: Compare Counterfactuals
description: Contrast realistic alternatives and trade-offs (e.g., policy vs. status quo) to clarify opportunity costs and likely outcomes under different choices.

name: Prebunk and Reframe
description: Anticipate common misconceptions with brief, factual corrections and reframe the issue around accurate mental models before myths take hold.

name: Actionable Next Steps
description: End with specific, low-friction actions and credible resources, reinforcing autonomy and making it easy to move from agreement to action.

name: Calibrated Consensus
description: Present the scientific or economic consensus with uncertainty ranges and major points of agreement, distinguishing settled facts from active debates to build credibility.

name: Steelman Their View
description: Restate the person’s position in its strongest form and acknowledge valid concerns before offering counterevidence, reducing defensiveness and encouraging open engagement.

name: Progressive Goalposts
description: Seek small, testable points of agreement first (definitions, basic facts), then iteratively build toward more contentious claims as common ground expands.

name: Interactive Evidence Dosing
description: Offer evidence in manageable chunks and ask for reactions after each, tailoring depth and sources to the person’s questions, knowledge level, and skepticism.

name: Counter-Mechanism Focus
description: Explain causal mechanisms (how and why) rather than only outcomes, using simple models or analogies; invite the person to propose alternative mechanisms and assess them together.

name: Agency and Next Steps
description: Conclude by offering actionable options aligned with their values and preferred level of engagement, reinforcing autonomy and reducing reactance.
